cells.tense: The exchange is even right now, and you can feel both ends of it.
cells.ask: Name what you are carrying for someone, then let them name what they carry for you. One round, no reply needed.
cells.core:
What you hand over and what comes back to you line up here, and you sit in both sides without flinching. You can say what you carry for someone else and what lands with you in return, and neither sentence costs you anything. Plenty of people can only hold one direction — pouring out or sitting in debt — and you are standing in both at the same time.

The sharing is the real kind, not a show put on for the room. It matters most where it runs through something the two of you keep and hand on: the way you do things, the thing people come to you for. What holds it steady is that you know where the ends land without running a tab. If this drifts, it won't be because you stopped offering. It'll be because one side quietly took on more and nobody said so.
cells.sheetLine: You trade fairly without keeping score, and it shows.
cells.verb: giving and receiving as they even out

cells.tense: You are living ahead of this exchange, watching for the moment the accounts come right.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you are owed or owe. Do nothing about it today, and mention it to no one.
cells.core:
You are tracking the fairness in this exchange harder than it is asking for. Somewhere ahead is a reckoning you can picture — who gives what, who gets what, what the numbers look like when it lands — and you are standing in that picture instead of this room. You offer a little past what is asked, and you keep a tally of who came up short and by how much. The tally is real work, and it eats the ease it was meant to buy.

What is on the other side is taking in without an itemised count. The strength that holds here is a holding, not a grip — you have it, you are just using it to press. In the next exchange you are in, give one thing and leave the total open. Let someone owe you for a while without either of you naming it.
cells.sheetLine: You are pressing for a reckoning instead of letting one land.

cells.tense: The exchange thinned out, and you are still giving from one side of it.
cells.ask: Write down one thing you handed over and still hold. Do not send it. Read it once, then put it away.
cells.core:
The ledger under this runs lopsided — you carry more than you let anyone carry for you, and expecting the other half has gone quiet. Taking something in has started to feel like a small threat. You accept carefully, or wave it off, or set it somewhere you won't have to look at it again. Offering continues because it long has. Receiving is the part that shut.

Generosity is not the gap here. Being able to let what is owed arrive is. Clear seeing moves that: weigh one exchange honestly instead of trusting the old tilt. Pick one thing you handed over that you still hold in your hands, and look straight at it. Then pick one thing someone is handing you now, and take it.
cells.sheetLine: You hand things over steadily and stopped expecting anything back.

cells.tense: The fair way is already running here, and you keep calling it just how things go.
cells.ask: Name one expectation you are holding in this exchange and say who it is held with.
cells.core:
You are already setting the terms of what people owe each other in this shared space — how much gets offered, what gets asked for, what counts as enough. It runs in the small moves: what you let pass, what you call out, who you decide has done their part. That is a real hand on the wheel, and it goes unnamed. You describe yourself as the one keeping things square, not the one deciding what square is.

Inside that, you see what is right long before you say it. It sits still instead of arguing — it just does not get spoken or drawn as a line. The exchange between you and the people here is in good shape. What is missing is you standing in the part you already play.
cells.sheetLine: You set what fair means here. You call it keeping things square.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim: that any of these sit in a specific person's history — the record gives a capacity in a seat, not a biography, so nothing about what happened, who, or how long ago can be said. A reader could fairly object that their exchange is with one institution rather than with people, or with family rather than a workplace; the picture has to be general enough to bend their direction. The ask survives being wrong because each one is an act inside this person's hand, not a prediction about the room it lands in. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is 'You always find the fair way' — it flatters the seat instead of saying what the seat is doing, so it is gone.
